title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
The core failure here is a system trained on copyrighted material without authorization from the rights holders. Udio's AI music generator allegedly reproduced protected elements of existing recordings closely enough that generated outputs resembled specific songs in melody, chord structure, and vocal arrangement. This is a training-data problem, not an inference-time moderation failure: the issue arose from what the model was built on, before any user ever typed a prompt.

The dispute involved multiple major rights holders and a separate class action brought by independent artists, indicating the alleged unauthorized use was not limited to a narrow set of recordings. Sony alleged more than 30,000 recordings were copied to train the models. UMG and Warner Music settled and moved to licensing agreements, while Sony filed a separate new lawsuit. A court allowed the independent artists' class action to proceed, though it transferred the case to a different jurisdiction. None of the lawsuits have reached a final verdict, and the allegations of copying are not established findings.

What would have caught this earlier is a rights-clearance process applied to training data before model development began, the same kind of check that governs licensed sampling in traditional music production. That step was either not taken or not taken fully. The settlements that followed, with their requirement that the platform retrain on licensed material only, effectively impose after the fact the standard that was absent at the outset.

summary:
# Summary

Universal Music Group has resolved its lawsuit against AI music startup Udio through licensing agreements. The dispute centered on Udio's use of copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system, which generates original music from text prompts. UMG claimed Udio created songs like "Sunshine Melody" that closely mimicked The Temptations' "My Girl," featuring similar melodies, chords, and backing vocals. Under the settlement, Udio will launch a new platform next year trained exclusively on authorized and licensed music, allowing users to customize and share their creations.

The agreement marks Udio's first licensing deal with a major music label and represents a shift in how the music industry approaches AI technology. UMG's CEO stated the settlement demonstrates commitment to both protecting artists and embracing new technologies. Udio, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees and backed by will.i.am and venture capital firms, has attracted millions of users since launching. The company will compensate artists who opt into the new platform, though specific financial terms and participating artists remain undisclosed. Additionally, UMG announced a partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers.
